tools.name: hub
tools.description:
Agent coordination: peer messaging, background-job control, and supervised long-running processes. Main agent is `Main`; subagents inherit task ID.
Use `op: "list"` to discover live peers. Default is running+idle plus running/idle/parked/shown/truncated counts — never an unbounded parked name dump. Pass `status: "parked"` for parked archaeology; optional `limit` bounds rows (default 32, max 100). Address peers by exact roster ID — NEVER invent names. `send` to a known parked id still revives it; `history://<id>` and `agent://<id>` stay readable.

# Messaging & Jobs

Background jobs auto-deliver when they finish. You NEVER need to poll. `jobs` is a non-consuming summary; `wait` observing a settled job first delivers its result and suppresses duplicate `async-result`.

- **The user is NOT a peer.** `Main` answers the user ONLY in a plain text block; a `send` shows them a tool-card preview (2 lines while collapsed). Thinking is not output either.
- **`send`** (with `to`): fire-and-forget, NEVER blocks. Delivery receipts (`delivered`/`failed`) immediate; `failed` → peer gone, don't retry.
  Sending wakes `idle`/`parked` peers. Answering: lead with answer, NEVER quote, set `replyTo`.
- **Format**: plain prose ONLY. No JSON status objects. Share paths via `local://`/`artifact://` URLs, not pasted blobs.
- **`wait`**: use ONLY when completely blocked with no other work. Returns on the FIRST of: an incoming message, a watched job finishing, the wait window elapsing (5s, lengthening with each back-to-back wait up to 5m), or a steering interrupt — NOT when all jobs finish; re-issue to keep waiting.
  - Any queued completion notice (an unwatched job finishing, a supervised process exiting) cuts every form of `wait` short as "skipped"; the notice lands on the next step. Re-issue the wait after handling it.
  - Bare `wait` watches every running job AND incoming messages. NEVER pass an array of every running ID; `ids` narrows to specific jobs, `from` to one peer (or use `await: true` on send).
  - A **user** message arriving as steering is not a wake reason to poll past: answer it in a text block BEFORE re-issuing `wait`. Parent/peer steering is answered with `send`; advisor and budget steers need no reply.
- **`inbox`**: drain queued messages without blocking.
- **`cancel`**: kill background jobs by `ids` when they have hung, stalled, or are no longer needed. Returns immediately.
- **`jobs`**: non-consuming status summary of every job. Use `wait` with an id to recover a settled result before auto-delivery. Also names running subagents with no job entry — coordinate with those via `send`.
- Job rows are process-local. A row whose result was delivered or recovered by a snapshot expires shortly (~30s) after; unconsumed rows stay inspectable for up to five minutes after settlement. Afterward, use the agent ID with `send`, `agent://<id>`, or `history://<id>`.
- `completed` means successful yield/job exit, not artifact acceptance. Verify claimed changes.
- NEVER use shell tools, grep, or read other sessions' files to figure out what a peer is doing. Message them directly.
- NEVER use hub messaging for something a tool can answer (e.g., grepping codebase, running a build).

# Processes

Project-scoped long-running processes shared by every omp instance in the same directory. A long-running service, watcher, debugger, REPL, or process needing later input MUST use `op:"start"`, not `bash`.

- **`start`** launches `application` + `args` directly. `cwd` defaults to the session directory; `pty` defaults true.
  - `ready.log` is a JavaScript `RegExp` compiled with the `u` flag; PCRE inline modifiers such as `(?i)` are REJECTED — use `[Rr]eady` instead. `ready.port` is a TCP port. Both supplied? BOTH MUST pass. `ready.timeout` is seconds. Readiness MUST be observed; process creation alone is not readiness.
  - Names are unique per project directory. A completed name MAY be started again; a live name MUST be stopped or restarted.
  - `restart` policy defaults `no`; `on-failure` and `always` use bounded backoff.
  - `persist: true` opts out of last-omp teardown; `detached: true` survives broker shutdown and all omp exits (implies persist, disables PTY input). Omit both unless their survival guarantees are required.
- **`ps`**, **`logs`**, **`wait`** (with `name`), **`send`** (with `name`), **`stop`**, **`restart`**, and **`describe`** address the stable `name`.
- **`logs`** defaults to the last 100 lines. `head: true` reads the beginning. `grep` is a JavaScript `RegExp` compiled with the `u` flag (no inline modifiers such as `(?i)`). `follow: true` waits for output after `cursor`; reuse the returned cursor on the next call.
- **`wait`** with `name` blocks until readiness/exit/`pattern` or `timeout` (seconds). `pattern` is a JavaScript `RegExp` compiled with the `u` flag (no inline modifiers such as `(?i)`). A `pattern` wait also returns when the process exits without ever printing it — check the reported state before assuming a match.
- **`send`** with `name`: `text` writes stdin (`enter` defaults true); `keys` supports ENTER, TAB, ESCAPE, CTRL_C, CTRL_D, UP, DOWN, LEFT, RIGHT; `signal` supports SIGINT, SIGTERM, SIGHUP, SIGQUIT, SIGKILL. PTY input is serialized; writes share one input stream.
- **`stop`** performs graceful process-tree termination before hard-kill; NEVER kill an unverified PID through bash. **`restart`** reuses the retained launch spec.

await.description: send: wait for the recipient's reply (invalid with to:"all")

from.description: wait: only accept a message from this agent id

ids.description: wait: job ids to watch (omit = all running jobs); cancel: job ids to kill

peek.description: inbox: list messages without consuming them

status.description: list: filter by status; omit for running+idle

limit.description: list: max peer rows; default 32, max 100

name.description: process ops: stable project-scoped launch name

args.description: start: argv passed directly to the application

cwd.description: start: working directory; defaults to the session directory

pty.description: start: allocate an interactive PTY; default true

port.description: TCP port that must accept connections

ready.description: start: readiness conditions; all supplied conditions must pass

persist.description: start: survive the last omp client exiting; default false

tools.name: todo
tools.description:
**Tasks: verbatim content strings, NEVER auto-generated IDs; no "task-1"/"task-N". Pass content in `task`.**

After each successful state-changing op: if nothing is `in_progress`, the earliest `pending` task (phase order) auto-promotes to `in_progress`; if several are `in_progress`, only the earliest stays. Blocked tasks NEVER auto-promote—`unblock` first. Out-of-order completion may move pointer back to an earlier phase—expected; completed tasks NEVER revert.

## Operations

|`op`|Fields|Effect|
|---|---|---|
|`init`|`list: [{phase, items: string[]}]`|Initialize full list; replaces existing|
|`init`|`items: string[]`|Flattened single-phase init|
|`start`|`task`|Mark in progress|
|`done`|`task` or `phase`|Mark completed|
|`drop`|`task` or `phase`|Mark abandoned|
|`block`|`task` or `phase`; optional `reason`|Mark blocked: awaiting external input; never auto-promotes; excluded from stop-time incomplete-todo reminder|
|`unblock`|`task` or `phase`|Blocked task → `pending`|
|`rm`|optional `task` or `phase`|Remove task/phase; omit both → clear|
|`append`|`phase`; `items: string[]`|Append tasks to phase; lazily creates phase|
|`view`|—|Read-only; echo list|

## Anatomy

- Task content: 5–10 words; what, not how; unique identifier.
- Phase name: short noun phrase (e.g. `Foundation`, `Auth`, `Verification`); unique identifier. NEVER prefix `1.`, `A)`, `Phase 1:`.

## Rules

- Mark tasks done immediately after finishing; complete phases in order.
- NEVER make a todo call the turn's only tool call. Batch with real work: `init` with first reads/edits; each `done`/`start` with next action. Solo todo turns waste a round trip.
- Waiting on something you can't act on—a user decision, another agent, external service: `block` task (optional `reason`); remains tracked but avoids stop reminder. Blocking the active task hands `in_progress` to the next `pending` task, never back to the blocked one. `unblock` when actionable. If blocker agent-actionable, `append` an unblocking task instead.
- Keep introduced `task`/`phase` strings stable.
- Lost exact task text: `view` echoes list; NEVER guess from memory.

## Create a list

- Task requires 3+ distinct steps.
- User explicitly requests one.
- User provides a set of tasks.
- New instructions arrive mid-task: capture before proceeding.

<critical>
User gives multi-step plan—phased todo, numbered/bulleted checklist, or "N bugs/items/tasks":
- MUST `init` every item as its own task before working.
- Enumerate all; NEVER summarize into fewer tasks, sample "the important ones", drop items, or track the rest from memory.
</critical>

items.description: tasks for single-phase init or append

Web search: current information beyond knowledge cutoff.

<instruction>
- SHOULD prefer primary sources (papers, official docs); corroborate key claims with multiple sources.
- MUST link cited sources in final response.
- NEVER use for programmatically accessible content or known URLs (GitHub repos/issues, known arXiv papers, Wikipedia pages, official docs) — `read` URL directly.
- `query`: every provider supports Google-style `site:`/`-site:`, `after:`/`before:` (`YYYY-MM-DD`), `inurl:`, `intitle:`, `filetype:`, `"exact phrase"`, `-term`, `OR`. Map constraints to native filters when available; otherwise filter results leniently. If a constraint matches nothing, relax and report it; do not return zero results.
</instruction>

tools.name: intercom
tools.description: Cross-session communication across the workspace: THE CHANNEL (realtime directed delivery) + THE LEDGER (the durable board every message lands on; hydra-v4.0 backend). THE TOGGLE LAW: sending TO a session AUTOMATICALLY SUBSCRIBES you to its messages; the subscription is DURABLE — NO TIMEOUT, NO EXPIRY — and stays on until you explicitly unsubscribe. So 'talk to X' turns the intercom on for X, and it stays on. Ops: list (who is live) · send (directed; auto-subscribes) · subscribe (to a session, without sending) · unsubscribe (one target, or ALL = the toggle off) · subscriptions (what you are subscribed to) · note (a thread entry, no recipient) · board (read the ledger) · who (thread members, present + departed) · inbox (drain what arrived — CHECK REGULARLY; inbound is a drain here) · status. Every send is recorded on the board in the same operation; every subscriber of the sender receives a copy. An unknown recipient is a loud refusal, never a silent drop.

to.description: send: the recipient sessionId or alias, or * to broadcast

tools.name: hydra_wave
tools.description: SUPERVISED wave dispatch over the hydra intercom: open a wave thread, assign tasks to workers, collect their reports on the durable board, steer them, and close with a verdict — all real-time over the shared rail. THE MANAGER spawns workers with its own task tool; this tool is the comms+ledger the wave runs on (every assignment and report lands on the board, so the manager steers live and a late joiner reads the whole wave). Ops: open (wave, subagents[]) · assign (wave, to, task) · report (wave, body) · status (wave, limit?) · steer (wave, to, directive) · close (wave, verdict).

tools.name: jev
tools.description: The local Jev decision engine: index a corpus, narrow it for FREE with keyless verbs, then ask a calibrated question about the survivors. USE THIS BEFORE DECIDING ANYTHING THAT IS A JUDGEMENT — classification, prioritisation, is-this-X, should-I-Y, which-of-N, how-confident — and BEFORE reading many files to find the few that matter. VERBS: index (build/refresh, keyless) · query (FTS/where, keyless) · scan (keyword+excerpt, keyless) · cluster (signature groups, keyless) · extract (regex -> structured rows, keyless) · report (index state, keyless) · filter (JUDGED narrowing with probabilities) · find (JUDGED 9-stage pattern chain) · decision-tree (JUDGED batch classification from a recipe) · route (JUDGED tool selection) · evaluate (JUDGED calibration) · push-gate / st-detect / spec-audit (mechanical gates). THE JUDGE IS LOCAL AND FREE — no api key, no billing, no quota; ~100ms warm, ~22s for 100 candidates in ONE request. ASK ONE THING: a compound 'X or Y' question caps the score below 0.5 and clears no real threshold. Sweep the threshold and read max/spread before you trust a min_p. READ THE TREND on find: 'N judged · 1 request' is healthy; 'N requests' means the endpoint is the llama.cpp backend, not the adapter.

i.description: one line: what you are looking for and why

fts.description: FTS5 MATCH phrase, e.g. theatrical or "exact phrase"

where.description: SQL predicate on the files row, e.g. size>20000

field.description: JSON field to pull (extract from jsonl/sqlite)

question.description: filter/route: ONE specific claim. Compound 'X or Y' questions score mid-range and clear nothing — state a single thing the text either is or is not

phrase.description: find: the X to hunt across the corpus

common.description: find: minimum support n for a pattern (default 2)

min_p.description: decision threshold. DERIVE it: sweep 0.2/0.4/0.6/0.8 and read max + spread. max < 0.5 means the QUESTION is broken, not the threshold

rows.description: decision-tree: rows file (json array or jsonl)

out.description: decision-tree: where to write the decisions

json.description: machine-readable stdout (stderr carries the cost line)

Runs Alibaba OpenCodeReview (ocr) over a diff or whole files and emits `GATE: PASS (0 critical/high)` or `GATE: FAIL (N critical, M high)` with file:line blockers. A FAIL blocks every ship-ready / production-grade / merge claim. Use before ANY completion claim on a code change. Quota/provider failure = BLOCKED, never a pass.

# Systematic Debugging

## Overview

**Core principle:** ALWAYS find root cause before attempting fixes. Symptom fixes are failure.

**Violating the letter of this process is violating the spirit of debugging.**

## The Iron Law

```
NO FIXES WITHOUT ROOT CAUSE INVESTIGATION FIRST
```

If you haven't completed Phase 1, you cannot propose fixes.

## When to Use

Use for ANY technical issue:
- Test failures
- Bugs in production
- Unexpected behavior
- Performance problems
- Build failures
- Integration issues

**Use this ESPECIALLY when:**
- Under time pressure (emergencies make guessing tempting)
- "Just one quick fix" seems obvious
- You've already tried multiple fixes
- Previous fix didn't work
- You don't fully understand the issue

**Don't skip when:**
- Issue seems simple (simple bugs have root causes too)
- You're in a hurry (rushing guarantees rework)
- Manager wants it fixed NOW (systematic is faster than thrashing)

## The Four Phases

You MUST complete each phase before proceeding to the next.

### Phase 1: Root Cause Investigation

**BEFORE attempting ANY fix:**

1. **Read Error Messages Carefully**
   - Don't skip past errors or warnings
   - They often contain the exact solution
   - Read stack traces completely
   - Note line numbers, file paths, error codes

2. **Reproduce Consistently**
   - Can you trigger it reliably?
   - What are the exact steps?
   - Does it happen every time?
   - If not reproducible → gather more data, don't guess

3. **Check Recent Changes**
   - What changed that could cause this?
   - Git diff, recent commits
   - New dependencies, config changes
   - Environmental differences

4. **Gather Evidence in Multi-Component Systems**

   **WHEN system has multiple components (CI → build → signing, API → service → database):**

   **BEFORE proposing fixes, add diagnostic instrumentation:**
   ```
   For EACH component boundary:
     - Log what data enters component
     - Log what data exits component
     - Verify environment/config propagation
     - Check state at each layer

   Run once to gather evidence showing WHERE it breaks
   THEN analyze evidence to identify failing component
   THEN investigate that specific component
   ```

   **Example (multi-layer system):**
   ```bash
   # Layer 1: Workflow
   echo "=== Secrets available in workflow: ==="
   echo "IDENTITY: ${IDENTITY:+SET}${IDENTITY:-UNSET}"

   # Layer 2: Build script
   echo "=== Env vars in build script: ==="
   env | grep IDENTITY || echo "IDENTITY not in environment"

   # Layer 3: Signing script
   echo "=== Keychain state: ==="
   security list-keychains
   security find-identity -v

   # Layer 4: Actual signing
   codesign --sign "$IDENTITY" --verbose=4 "$APP"
   ```

   **This reveals:** Which layer fails (secrets → workflow ✓, workflow → build ✗)

5. **Trace Data Flow**

   **WHEN error is deep in call stack:**

   See `root-cause-tracing.md` in this directory for the complete backward tracing technique.

   **Quick version:**
   - Where does bad value originate?
   - What called this with bad value?
   - Keep tracing up until you find the source
   - Fix at source, not at symptom

### Phase 2: Pattern Analysis

**Find the pattern before fixing:**

1. **Find Working Examples**
   - Locate similar working code in same codebase
   - What works that's similar to what's broken?

2. **Compare Against References**
   - If implementing pattern, read reference implementation COMPLETELY
   - Don't skim - read every line
   - Understand the pattern fully before applying

3. **Identify Differences**
   - What's different between working and broken?
   - List every difference, however small
   - Don't assume "that can't matter"

4. **Understand Dependencies**
   - What other components does this need?
   - What settings, config, environment?
   - What assumptions does it make?

### Phase 3: Hypothesis and Testing

**Scientific method:**

1. **Form Single Hypothesis**
   - State clearly: "I think X is the root cause because Y"
   - Write it down
   - Be specific, not vague

2. **Test Minimally**
   - Make the SMALLEST possible change to test hypothesis
   - One variable at a time
   - Don't fix multiple things at once

3. **Verify Before Continuing**
   - Did it work? Yes → Phase 4
   - Didn't work? Form NEW hypothesis
   - DON'T add more fixes on top

4. **When You Don't Know**
   - Say "I don't understand X"
   - Don't pretend to know
   - Ask for help
   - Research more

### Phase 4: Implementation

**Fix the root cause, not the symptom:**

1. **Create Failing Test Case**
   - Simplest possible reproduction
   - Automated test if possible
   - One-off test script if no framework
   - MUST have before fixing
   - Use the `superpowers:test-driven-development` skill for writing proper failing tests

2. **Implement Single Fix**
   - Address the root cause identified
   - ONE change at a time
   - No "while I'm here" improvements
   - No bundled refactoring

3. **Verify Fix**
   - Test passes now?
   - No other tests broken?
   - Issue actually resolved?
   - Use the `superpowers:verification-before-completion` skill before claiming success

4. **If Fix Doesn't Work**
   - STOP
   - Count: How many fixes have you tried?
   - If < 3: Return to Phase 1, re-analyze with new information
   - **If ≥ 3: STOP and question the architecture (step 5 below)**
   - DON'T attempt Fix #4 without architectural discussion

5. **If 3+ Fixes Failed: Question Architecture**

   **Pattern indicating architectural problem:**
   - Each fix reveals new shared state/coupling/problem in different place
   - Fixes require "massive refactoring" to implement
   - Each fix creates new symptoms elsewhere

   **STOP and question fundamentals:**
   - Is this pattern fundamentally sound?
   - Are we "sticking with it through sheer inertia"?
   - Should we refactor architecture vs. continue fixing symptoms?

   **Discuss with your human partner before attempting more fixes**

   This is NOT a failed hypothesis - this is a wrong architecture.

## Red Flags - STOP and Follow Process

If you catch yourself thinking:
- "Quick fix for now, investigate later"
- "Just try changing X and see if it works"
- "Add multiple changes, run tests"
- "Skip the test, I'll manually verify"
- "It's probably X, let me fix that"
- "I don't fully understand but this might work"
- "Pattern says X but I'll adapt it differently"
- "Here are the main problems: [lists fixes without investigation]"
- Proposing solutions before tracing data flow
- **"One more fix attempt" (when already tried 2+)**
- **Each fix reveals new problem in different place**

**ALL of these mean: STOP. Return to Phase 1.**

**If 3+ fixes failed:** Question the architecture (see Phase 4.5)

## your human partner's Signals You're Doing It Wrong

**Watch for these redirections:**
- "Is that not happening?" - You assumed without verifying
- "Will it show us...?" - You should have added evidence gathering
- "Stop guessing" - You're proposing fixes without understanding
- "Ultra-think this" - Question fundamentals, not just symptoms
- "We're stuck?" (frustrated) - Your approach isn't working

**When you see these:** STOP. Return to Phase 1.

## Common Rationalizations

|Excuse|Reality|
|---|---|
|"Issue is simple, don't need process"|Simple issues have root causes too. Process is fast for simple bugs.|
|"Emergency, no time for process"|Systematic debugging is FASTER than guess-and-check thrashing.|
|"Just try this first, then investigate"|First fix sets the pattern. Do it right from the start.|
|"I'll write test after confirming fix works"|Untested fixes don't stick. Test first proves it.|
|"Multiple fixes at once saves time"|Can't isolate what worked. Causes new bugs.|
|"Reference too long, I'll adapt the pattern"|Partial understanding guarantees bugs. Read it completely.|
|"I see the problem, let me fix it"|Seeing symptoms ≠ understanding root cause.|
|"One more fix attempt" (after 2+ failures)|3+ failures = architectural problem. Question pattern, don't fix again.|

## Quick Reference

|Phase|Key Activities|Success Criteria|
|---|---|---|
|**1. Root Cause**|Read errors, reproduce, check changes, gather evidence|Understand WHAT and WHY|
|**2. Pattern**|Find working examples, compare|Identify differences|
|**3. Hypothesis**|Form theory, test minimally|Confirmed or new hypothesis|
|**4. Implementation**|Create test, fix, verify|Bug resolved, tests pass|

## When Process Reveals "No Root Cause"

If systematic investigation reveals issue is truly environmental, timing-dependent, or external:

1. You've completed the process
2. Document what you investigated
3. Implement appropriate handling (retry, timeout, error message)
4. Add monitoring/logging for future investigation

**But:** 95% of "no root cause" cases are incomplete investigation.

## Supporting Techniques

These techniques are part of systematic debugging and available in this directory:

- **`root-cause-tracing.md`** - Trace bugs backward through call stack to find original trigger
- **`defense-in-depth.md`** - Add validation at multiple layers after finding root cause
- **`condition-based-waiting.md`** - Replace arbitrary timeouts with condition polling

---
name: omp-extension-tool-invisible-diagnosis
description: "Diagnose an OMP extension tool that LOADS fine but never appears in a session's tool schema — the three real defects (loadMode defaulting to discoverable→xd:// mount, required i stripped by the harness, resumed sessions restoring their own active set). Use when a fresh boot works but a session lacks the tool, when a tool is xd://-only, when every call fails \"i was missing\", or before rebuilding an extension that is actually wired correctly."
---

# OMP extension tool invisible — the three-defect diagnosis chain

An extension tool can be fully loaded, registered, and executing — and still absent from the model's schema. Diagnose in this order; each step has a mechanical probe.

## Probe 0 — the tool is often NOT missing

Read the xd:// device path FIRST: `read(path="xd://<toolname>")`. If it returns the tool's schema, **the extension loaded and the tool is registered** — it is merely presented as discoverable. This one read prevents a full rebuild of working code.

Also: a model's self-report ("TOOL-ABSENT") is NOT an instrument. It reported TOOL-ABSENT while its transcript showed the tool present and the model calling it. ALWAYS verify via the session transcript: `grep -c '"name":"<tool>"' <session.jsonl>` — the tool schema materializes in request payloads once one request completes.

## Defect 1 — loadMode defaults to "discoverable"

Contract (pi-coding-agent `extensibility/extensions/types.ts`): *"Extension tools default to `discoverable`; set `essential` to stay top-level."* Discoverable tools get mounted under `xd://` (setting `tools.xdev`, default true) instead of shipping their schema on every request.

Working reference shape (copy it exactly):
```js
pi.registerTool({
  name: "x",
  label: "x",
  loadMode: "essential",
  defaultInactive: false,
  description: "...",
  parameters: ...,
  async execute(...) {...},
});
```
Verify the consumer: `defaultLoadModeForToolName(name, declared)` returns `declared` when set — explicit essential always wins.

## Defect 2 — a required `i` parameter dies in the call path

`i` is the harness's intent field. Observed mechanically: the model SENT `{"i":"...","verb":"report"}`, the tool RECEIVED `{"verb":"report"}`, validation failed `"i ... (was missing)"` on every call.

Rule: never make `i` required on an extension tool. Write `i: z.string().optional().describe(...)` or omit it. Any required field that the call path can consume = 100% call failure with a cryptic validation error.

## Defect 3 — resumed sessions restore their own active set

A fresh session gets `!defaultInactive` extension tools auto-included. A RESUMED session restores its saved active set — a tool newer than that state stays inactive (xd:// fallback) even with `loadMode: "essential"`.

The contract says the registering extension owns activation: *"The registering extension is responsible for activating/deactivating it via setActiveTools()."* `pi.setActiveTools` exists on the ExtensionAPI and binds only after session construction — so hook `session_start`:
```js
pi.on("session_start", async () => {
  try {
    const active = pi.getActiveTools();
    if (!active.includes("x")) await pi.setActiveTools([...active, "x"]);
  } catch {}
});
```

## The verification chain (all mechanical)

1. Harness: fake `pi` with `zod`, `registerTool` (capture), `on` (capture), `getActiveTools`, `setActiveTools`; fire the captured `session_start` handler and assert the tool name lands in `setActiveTools`.
2. Fresh boot: boot a fresh omp via hub, drive one call, read the session jsonl for the toolResult and `Validation failed` count (want 0).
3. Resumed-session proof: boot `omp --resume <dead-session-id>` (back the file up first, restore after), drive one call, grep the transcript for `"name":"<tool>"`.
4. Observability: add `console.log("[<ext>] registered <tool>")` in the factory — `pi.log` does NOT exist on the real API (it has `logger`, an object); `pi.log?.()` is a silent no-op.

## Traps

- Same file, same config, different behavior across sessions → check `loadMode` + session resume state, not the config.
- No error notification for a silently-inactive tool is normal — it is not a load failure.
- A model on a fresh boot may fail with a 429 quota error; that is the MODEL, not the wiring — switch models per the rate-limit law.
- The extension file's mtime query (`?mtime=`) cache-busts per load; a fresh process gets the current file — no stale-module excuse.

## Workflows verdict (short — full proof in the reference)

OMP does **not** ship built-in deterministic workflows like MiMo-Code
(`compose`, `deep-research`, `fact-check`, `research-experiment` behind
the `workflow` tool and `.mimocode/workflows/*.js`) or Qwen-Code (saved
`.qwen/workflows/*.js` via the `workflow` tool plus the
`workflow-creator` skill, exposed as `/<name>`). Mechanical evidence on
this host: 92 tool files under `src/tools/` contain no workflow/compose
file; `grep workflow` over `src/tools/` hits only GitHub-Actions
`workflow_runs` renderers; `dist/types/modes/workflow.d.ts` is only the
`workflowz` magic-keyword highlighter, not a tool. The OMP-native way to
run the same shapes is the persistent `eval` kernel (`agent()`,
`parallel()`, `pipeline()`, `workpool()`, `wait()`, `completion()`) plus
`task`-batch fan-out plus the `workflowz` contract, with autoresearch and
goals covering the experiment/goal loops. Read
`references/workflows-vs-mimo-qwen.md` before telling any user how to
"run a workflow" on OMP — it carries the per-system API tables and the
porting map.

- Changing a behavior: `omp config list | grep <key>`, `omp config get <key>`, `omp config set <key> <value>`; scopes are global agent-dir vs project cwd. Never invent keys — `references/runtime-map.md` lists the real ones.
- Skills: one dir per skill `<root>/skills/<name>/SKILL.md` with `name` + `description` frontmatter; native roots are `~/.omp/agent/skills/` (user) and `<cwd>/.omp/skills/` walking up (project); `skills.customDirectories` scans non-recursively. Reach via `skill://<name>`, `/skill:<name>`.
- Slash commands: `~/.omp/agent/commands/*.md` (user) and `<cwd>/.omp/commands/*.md` (project); body uses `$ARGUMENTS` / `$1` / `$@`; ends with `$ARGUMENTS`.

- Eval fan-out: one cell per `eval` call, state persists per language; `agent()` returns text or `{ text, handle, id }` with `handle:true`; failures resolve `null`, never throw; barriers settle every item before returning.
- Embed via SDK: `bun add @oh-my-pi/pi-coding-agent`, `createAgentSession()` with auto-discovery, `session.subscribe` for `message_update/text_delta`, `session.prompt(...)`, `session.dispose()`. Full contract in `references/sdk-essentials.md`.
- Debug TUI/rendering/SSH: upstream `docs/tui.md`, `docs/compaction.md`; prefer local render + remote `serve`-side execution patterns over raw SSH TUI.

## Where Things Live On Disk

- Binary: `/home/leviathan/.bun/bin/omp` (bundled `dist/cli.js` + native `.node`).
- Package sources on this host: `/home/leviathan/node_modules/@oh-my-pi/pi-coding-agent/` (`src/`, `dist/types/`, `examples/sdk/`, `examples/extensions/`, `examples/hooks/`).
- User agent dir (default profile): `~/.omp/agent/` — `skills/`, `commands/`, `agents/`, `extensions/`, `managed-skills/`, `sessions/`, `config.yml`, `models.yml`, `mcp.json`.

- Project roots: `<cwd>/.omp/` — `skills/`, `commands/`, `agents/`.
- Cross-harness mirrors (foreign providers, opt-in): `~/.claude/`, `<cwd>/.claude/`, `~/.codex/`, `.opencode/`, `.agent[s]/`, `.github/skills/`.
- This skill: `~/.omp/agent/skills/omp-docs/SKILL.md` + `references/`; command: `~/.omp/agent/commands/omp-docs.md`.

## Commands

`omp` subcommands include `acp`, `agents`, `auth-broker`, `browser-relay`, `cleanse`, `commit`, `completions`, `config`, `models`, `plugin`, `read`, `grep`, `search`, `share`, `join`, `stats`, `usage`, `worktree`, `ttsr`, `setup`, `update`. Unknown `/...` falls through as literal prompt text — never claim rejection.

## Helping the User Configure

1. Identify the exact schema field from `references/runtime-map.md` or `omp config list`. Do not infer keys from MiMoCode/Qwen formats.
2. Scope from the request: model/provider setup is global unless repo-local behavior is explicit; use project `.omp` only for repo-local behavior.
3. Inspect only the exact config candidates. Redact `apiKey`, `token`, `secret`, `password` values; never dump whole credential files to find a shape.
4. Edit minimally: `omp config set <key> <value>`; preserve unrelated keys.
5. Validate with the narrowest command (`omp config get <key>`, a one-cell `eval`, a `/skill:<name>` smoke) and report files changed + whether a relaunch is needed.
6. If no key exists for the behavior, say so and suggest the closest supported option or a custom tool/hook/extension — never invent a key.

## Answering Feature Questions

- Confirm the feature exists in the map above before describing it.
- Give the trigger (command / key / config), then a one-line how.
- For deterministic multi-agent orchestration, teach eval-`agent()` + `task` batch + `workflowz` — never describe a `workflow` tool, `compose` builtin, or saved-workflow directory as if OMP had one.
- For new tools/hooks/skills/extensions, point at `examples/custom-tools/`, `examples/hooks/`, `examples/extensions/`, and upstream `docs/extensions.md` / `docs/custom-tools.md`.
- If unsure whether a detail is current, verify against `src/` or `dist/types/` on disk rather than asserting.

## Evidence law

Every claim about OMP behavior cites the command plus its output or the
source file plus lines. Prose is not proof. `omp.sh/docs` SPA-shell
fetches are never evidence of content — quote the upstream raw `docs/`
file or the on-disk `src/` path instead.
